questions.question: What is the most common reason a prompt works in testing but fails in production?
options: The model gets updated too frequently
Real users send inputs the prompt was never tested against — edge cases, empty fields, mixed languages
Production servers run the model at higher temperature
The prompt exceeds token limits in production
questions.explanation: A prompt tested on a few typical examples often breaks on boundary cases. Production prompt engineering means testing what happens when input is empty, malformed, or unexpected.

questions.question: Why is 'Classify this ticket' a weak prompt for an IT ticket classifier?
options: It's too short for the model to process
It gives no categories, no format, and no guidance for ambiguous cases
It doesn't mention which model to use
It needs to be in all caps
questions.explanation: Without explicit categories, a fallback, and an output format, the model guesses — and it will guess differently for different inputs.

questions.question: Where should your core instructions live for maximum reliability?
options: In the user message, repeated each time
In a separate document the model retrieves
questions.explanation: System prompts are more reliable than per-message instructions. Keep core instructions in the system prompt; use user messages for the actual data.

questions.question: When should you consider fine-tuning instead of adding more instructions to a prompt?
options: When the behavior is hard to describe in words but easy to show with many examples
When the model is too slow
When you want to switch to a smaller model
questions.explanation: Prompts are best for behavior you can articulate. Fine-tuning is better when the pattern is implicit and would require an unwieldy number of examples in the prompt.
